title: Make Your Phone Less Visually Tempting with Grayscale
subtitle: A reversible interface nudge for reducing habitual screen time
description: If you want to spend less time on your phone, try switching the display to grayscale for a bounded trial. Treat it as friction against habitual use, not as a productivity, sleep, or mental-health upgrade.

lifeOsSource.hack: Turn your smartphone display to grayscale when your goal is to make habitual phone use slightly less rewarding and easier to interrupt.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Enable grayscale on your phone and leave the rest of your normal setup alone for a bounded trial. Use the phone when you actually need it; the point is not abstinence. Notice whether automatic checking becomes less attractive. If color is important for navigation, accessibility, work, photos, or another real task, switch color back on for that task instead of treating grayscale as a purity test.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did my phone screen time or automatic checking change, and did I simply move the same distraction to another device?
lifeOsSource.reference: Hagerty et al. (2026) — Cross-over feasibility trial of smartphone grayscale mode

faq.question: Does grayscale improve productivity?
faq.answer: That is not established here. The 2026 trial found lower smartphone screen time, while exploratory productivity and sleep measures did not show consistent significant differences. Use grayscale for screen-time friction, not as a general performance claim.

faq.question: Do I need to keep the phone grayscale all day?
faq.answer: No. Color can be functional. If a map, chart, photo, accessibility feature, or work task depends on color, use color. The useful experiment is whether reducing visual salience during ordinary discretionary use changes your behavior.

faq.question: How long should I test it?
faq.answer: There is no established universal dose. The reviewed study used one-week conditions, but that does not make one week optimal. Choose a bounded period that includes ordinary days and compare what actually happens.

faq.question: What if I just use my laptop more?
faq.answer: Count that as useful information. Participants in the study also described substitution to other devices. The goal is not to win a screen-time statistic; it is to reduce the behavior you actually want to reduce.

intro.html: A phone can be distracting without being forbidden. Grayscale changes the interface rather than blocking access. In a 2026 cross-over feasibility trial, 51 first-year medical students used grayscale and normal color displays in consecutive one-week conditions. Average daily smartphone screen time was about 28 minutes lower during grayscale. That is a useful signal, but the study was small, short, unblinded, and based on participants reporting the screen-time value shown by their phones. Brali therefore treats grayscale as a cheap, reversible nudge to test—not as a cure for digital distraction.

sections.title: 1. Be clear about the target
sections.html: Use this protocol when the problem is habitual phone engagement: opening feeds without deciding to, staying longer than intended, or repeatedly checking because the device is visually inviting. If your screen time is mostly navigation, calls, study tools, accessibility software, or work you genuinely need to do, a lower number is not automatically an improvement.

sections.title: 2. Change one environmental variable
sections.html: Turn on grayscale and avoid adding five other digital-detox rules at the same time. A one-variable experiment is easier to understand. You can still open every app. The intervention simply removes much of the color that contributes to visual salience.

sections.title: 3. Let useful color stay useful
sections.html: Color carries information. Maps, photographs, charts, status indicators, design work, and some accessibility needs can become worse in grayscale. Switch back when color has a job. A sensible intervention removes unnecessary attraction without making the device unnecessarily hard to use.

sections.title: 4. Watch for substitution
sections.html: A lower phone total can hide the same behavior on a laptop, tablet, or television. One participant in the reviewed study explicitly described this. If the distraction simply moves, the experiment has still taught you something: the problem is broader than the phone's color palette.

sections.title: 5. Review behavior, not mythology
sections.html: At the end of the trial, compare ordinary phone use with your baseline. Did automatic checking feel less attractive? Did screen time change? Did anything important become harder? The study did not show a reliable productivity or sleep benefit, and it cannot tell us whether the effect lasts for months. Keep grayscale only if the small amount of friction is useful in your real life.

references.title: A cross-over feasibility trial of smartphone grayscale mode in medical students
references.claim_scope: Supports a preliminary association between grayscale display use and lower daily smartphone screen time in a two-week cross-over feasibility trial of 51 first-year medical students. It does not establish durable effects, a universal screen-time reduction, or reliable improvements in productivity, sleep, or mental health.

editorialCuration.reason: Create a narrow Digital Attention protocol from a fully reviewed 2026 cross-over feasibility trial. The public protocol keeps the demonstrated endpoint—smartphone screen time—and explicitly excludes unsupported productivity, sleep, mental-health, long-term, and universal-effect claims.
